pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, answered about their own project with concrete commands, files and numbers; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Which gates does your pipeline run, when does it run them, and what actually stops a red branch from being merged?
expected_points: build, test with -race, vet, and govulncheck — each one named with what it catches
triggers on push and on proposed merges, so the check runs before the merge rather than after it
blocking is a repository setting (required status checks on the protected branch), not a line in the workflow file
a flaky gate teaches everyone to press re-run, so red must always mean broken
the pipeline runs on a clean machine, which is what proves nothing depends on their laptop

questions.prompt: Walk me through deploying a new version of your project, and then rolling it back. What in your Dockerfile makes the artifact trustworthy?
expected_points: the steps are in a file (script, Makefile target, manifests) and were run as written, not from memory
immutable versioned artifact: build once, tag it, promote that image; never rebuild the same tag
multi-stage build with a pinned base tag or digest and a non-root USER in the final stage — latest means the image debugged is not the image shipped
rollback is one rehearsed command, run before the incident is understood, with a known duration
an honest list of what rollback cannot undo (migrations, consumed messages, published releases) and what the forward fix is instead

questions.prompt: Your project is misbehaving and you cannot read the code or attach a debugger. Using only telemetry, how do you establish whether it is healthy, how badly it is failing, and since when?
expected_points: metrics say something is wrong, traces say where, logs say what
structured logs with fixed keys so lines can be counted and filtered, not just read
counters over a metrics surface (expvar or a client library) covering rate, errors and duration
'since when' comes from a series over time, which is why a log-only answer is incomplete
any question they could only answer by reading source is a gap in instrumentation, not a gap in luck

questions.prompt: Your process gets SIGTERM one second into a five-second request during a rollout. What happens, in order? And what is the difference between your health and readiness endpoints?
expected_points: catch the signal (signal.NotifyContext with os.Interrupt and SIGTERM) — a rollout, scale-down or restart always begins with SIGTERM
fail readiness first so the load balancer stops routing new work, then drain
srv.Shutdown(ctx) with a bounded timeout lets in-flight requests finish; then close what you own and exit with a meaningful code
liveness means 'restart me' and stays dumb; readiness means 'stop sending me work' without a restart
the shutdown timeout must be shorter than the platform's termination grace period or SIGKILL lands mid-drain

questions.prompt: I am on call at 3am, you are unreachable, and your service is down. Open your runbook: what does it tell me to do, and how do you know it is true?
expected_points: deploy, rollback, what to check when it is down, and who to page — with literal commands, not prose
the triage section is ordered cheapest and most likely first, and says how to read each answer
two failure modes specific to this system: symptom, the check that confirms it, cause, action
it is true because they followed it themselves during the rollback and telemetry rehearsals and fixed every improvisation
'me, and nobody else' is an acceptable paging answer only with what happens when they are unreachable

questions.prompt: Someone deploys your project with a typo in one environment variable. What happens, and how did they know the variable existed?
expected_points: configuration is validated at startup and the process fails loudly, so the rollout fails while the old version still serves
a silently substituted default turns a typo into an outage that starts hours later
defaults that run: the program starts with no configuration at all
every knob is documented with name, meaning, default and whether it is a secret; the referee cross-checks os.Getenv against the docs
secrets arrive the same way and then never appear in logs, errors, metric labels or crash dumps

questions.prompt: Name two operational choices in your project that limit blast radius, and one that could still take something down beyond your service.
expected_points: non-root, minimal runtime image: a container escape does not start as root and has no shell or package manager to use
readiness separate from liveness: a slow dependency drains traffic instead of restarting the whole fleet
a metric label with unbounded values (user id, path, error text) can take down the metrics backend — S5's cardinality bomb
a liveness probe that checks a dependency turns one dependency blip into a fleet-wide restart
awareness that some failures are external to the process and are handled by rollback plus a runbook, not by code
